title: The Priestly Divisions
lead: The priests of the Jerusalem temple served in twenty-four rotating divisions, or courses, each on duty for a week at a time. Chronicles traces the system to David; it lasted until the temple fell in AD 70 and is assumed in Luke's story of Zechariah, father of John the Baptist.

sections.b: Chronicles traces the twenty-four courses to David (1 Chronicles 24). After the exile, Nehemiah's lists of priestly families share many of their names (Nehemiah 10:2–8; 12:1–21). In the second temple each course served for a week at a time. Mattathias, who began the Maccabean revolt, came from the first course (1 Maccabees 2:1), and so did Josephus (Life 1–2), who says David's arrangement lasted to his own day (Antiquities 7.365–366). Calendar texts from Qumran (4Q320–330) set the courses in a solar year. The Mishnah pairs each course with a delegation of ordinary Israelites (Mishnah Taanit 4:2). Luke sets the promise of John the Baptist's birth during the week of the course of Abijah (Luke 1:5–9). After AD 70 the courses were remembered with their home towns in Galilee in synagogue inscriptions, such as one from Caesarea, and in liturgical poems.
